beats.say: Eight CDs for a penny. And you still pay later.
Get the penny starter, then you owe a set number of albums at full price.
Skip the penny, just buy albums when you want, no hidden commitment.
Pick the premium plan, pay more upfront, no surprise shipments.
Members who never declined still got the next CD billed. Sounds generous.
But it does a job: a negative-option trap.
The cheap penny option forces you into a contract.
If you miss the decline window, the next selection auto-ships and charges you.
Revenue hit $1.4 billion in 1996, then fell to $17 million by 2014.
You see it everywhere - a gym offers a $1 trial, then requires a $30 monthly membership.
A streaming app gives a free month, then auto-renews at $12 unless you cancel.
The pushed monthly plan feels reasonable because the initial free offer disappears.
Check the opt-out deadline; a tiny upfront cost may conceal larger fees. Follow for more.
